title: Convergence Economics
subtitle: The mechanisms, constraints, incentives and policies governing convergence between economies
description: Proposes Convergence Economics as a field and tests its core claims on public data: seven kinds of convergence, eight mechanisms, binding constraints and the arithmetic of catch-up speed.
contribution: Defines Convergence Economics, audits eight mechanisms across 76 developing economies and sets out constraints, incentives, policy levers, speed scenarios to 2100 and ten testable propositions.
abstract: Whether poorer economies will catch up with richer ones has been asked for two centuries, yet no single field integrates the answer. This report proposes Convergence Economics, the study of the mechanisms, conditions, constraints, incentives and policies that govern the narrowing of economic disparities between countries, and tests its core claims against public data. Between 2000 and 2024, Global South income rose from 13% to 24% of the high-income level, but only from 18% to 20% without China and India, while low-income countries slipped from 4.2% to 3.7%. Sustained catch-up is rare: just 20% of 25-year windows for lagging economies show a growth advantage of two points a year or more.

Convergence is plural. Across seven dimensions (productivity, technology, structure, capital, human capital, institutions and infrastructure, sustainability), changes are only weakly correlated (mean rank correlation 0.20). An audit of 76 developing economies finds no single mechanism sufficient. Even in the top third on the strongest mechanism, 23% failed to converge, whereas 90% of economies strong on five or six of eight mechanisms did converge. Only 2 of 10 tested complementarities are significant. The industrial route has narrowed, and binding constraints in debt service, power and governance limit speed. At a steady two-point annual advantage, the Global South would reach half of the high-income level in about 38 years and low-income countries in 130. The report closes with ten testable propositions and a research programme built on open data.
coreProposition: Convergence is plural, conditional and slow: it happens through combinations of mechanisms, within limits set by finance, capacity, power, population and climate, and through incentives that can be aligned or not.

keyFindings.title: Real but narrow, and period-dependent.
keyFindings.text: Global South income rose from 13% to 24% of the high-income level in 2000–2024, but only from 18% to 20% without China and India; low-income countries slipped from 4.2% to 3.7%. Of 99 developing economies, 71% outgrew high-income countries in 2000–19 but only 48% in 2019–24.

keyFindings.title: Sustained catch-up is rare.
keyFindings.text: Only 20% of 25-year windows for lagging economies show a growth advantage of two points a year or more, and 10% show three. Of 99 economies below a quarter of US income in 1960, 76 were still below it in 2022.

keyFindings.title: Convergence comes in seven kinds.
keyFindings.text: Changes across productivity, technology, structure, capital, human capital, institutions and infrastructure, and sustainability have a mean rank correlation of only 0.20. Only 4 of 62 economies narrowed the gap on all eight dimensions.

keyFindings.title: No single mechanism is sufficient.
keyFindings.text: Even in the top third on the strongest mechanism, 23% of 76 economies failed to converge. The share that converged rises from 32% (strong on 0–2 of eight mechanisms) to 90% (strong on 5–6), though the audit is descriptive and the top group is small.

keyFindings.title: Complementarity is real but not simple.
keyFindings.text: Only 2 of 10 tested pairings show a significant interaction, and in one of them the mechanism matters less where its supposed complement is strong. The evidence favours bundles over single gates.

keyFindings.title: The industrial route has narrowed.
keyFindings.text: The predicted manufacturing share of GDP at ,000 of income fell from 17% in the 1990s to 13% in 2015–19, and the share fell in 47 of 82 developing economies after 2000. Resource booms, not manufacturing, dominate the fastest 25-year catch-up windows.

keyFindings.title: Finance and power bind hardest.
keyFindings.text: Median interest payments take 13% of government revenue in low-income countries, up from 3% in 2010, and electricity use is 170 kWh per person against 8,804 in high-income countries.

keyFindings.title: The clock is long.
keyFindings.text: At a steady two-point annual advantage the Global South reaches half of the high-income level in about 38 years, lower-middle-income countries in 62 and low-income countries in 130. The scenarios are arithmetic illustrations, not forecasts.

keyFindings.title: Ten testable propositions.
keyFindings.text: Five find first support in the report's data, four are partly supported or mixed and one (finance) is untested. The report presents the field as a proposed framework open to testing and notes that the phrase has been used before in a narrower sense (De Grauwe, 1996).

bottomLine: A data-grounded case for treating convergence as a field. Its statistical results are descriptive associations on small samples, its scenarios are constant-advantage arithmetic, and the report says so itself.

glossary.definition: The study of the mechanisms, conditions, constraints and policies governing the reduction of economic disparities between countries and regions, with emphasis on how developing economies approach the productivity, technology, income and productive sophistication of advanced economies.
The seven dimensions along which an economy can close its gap with the frontier: productivity, technology, structure, capital, human capital, institutions and infrastructure, and sustainability.
Technology diffusion, capital accumulation, human capital development, industrialization, international trade, foreign direct investment, institutional development and infrastructure investment.
The test of whether economies that start poorer grow faster, estimated as the slope of growth on initial log income.
The annual difference in log income per person between a developing economy and the high-income average; "converged" here means at least one point a year over 2000–19.
The pattern in which latecomer economies reach their peak manufacturing share earlier and at lower income than earlier industrializers.
A limit whose relaxation would raise growth most, while relaxing others would raise it little.
The skills, management, institutions and infrastructure that determine whether imported technology and capital become productivity.
The number of the eight mechanisms in which an economy ranks in the top third, used to show that convergence is a property of bundles.
The 75th (about 1.6 points a year) and 90th (about 3 points a year) percentiles of the growth advantage sustained over 25 years by lagging economies.
A country-year in which income per person falls; used as an indicator of how exposed convergence is to shocks.
